messages.author: 2e220ee4f483b215
messages.subject: Operative temperature
parts:
Hi! 

I am fairly new to using NichMapR, and I was wondering the best way to get the operative temperature from the ectotherm model. I am trying to get the operative temperatures in total sun and total shade (90%), and my approach was to manipulate the various temperature parameters so that the organisms is in constant shade or sun. When comparing the results with a different biophysical model, the operative temperatures in the shade are very similar, but my in the sun operative temperatures are pretty low. Is there a certain way to set the temperature parameters? or is there a better approach to obtaining operative temperatures?

Thanks you for the help!
-Julie

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Operative temperature
parts:
Hi Julie,

If you set 'live = 0', it will turn off all behaviours and metabolic heat production as well as evaporative water loss. I think this will give you what you want. (I might change the model so evaporative water loss is not turned off)

Also, if you do this before calling the ectotherm model, the animal will be in the shaded scenario:

micro$metout <- micro$shadmet
micro$soil <- micro$shadsoil

All the best,
Mike

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Operative temperature
parts:
Hi Mi,

It's "TC". Operative temperature is the 'steady state' temperature some object would reach if held indefinitely in a given environment, and this is essentially what the model is predicting. It's the same as what you'd get with a low heat capacity physical model of the organism, e.g. one made of copper, so it changes temperature almost instantly as the environment changes (e.g. as the sun comes out from behind a cloud). I.e. it isn't accounting for the object lagging behind the temperature its environment is driving it towards, because of rapid changes in the environment. For many small organisms, and many questions, the steady state or operative temperatures provided by the 'ectotherm' model are fine. But if you want to account for the lag, then you can use the 'transient' models ('onelump', 'onelump_var' and 'twolump_var'), e.g. see http://bioforecasts.science.unimelb.edu.au/app_direct/ectotherm_transient/

All the best,
Mike

messages.author: e46cb5dd353b7dfb
messages.subject: Re: Operative temperature
parts:
Hi Mi,

Yes that will give you the operative temperature of a non-thermoregulating object under the minimum shade scenario, but even with behavioural thermoregulation turned on the model is predicting operative temperatures, just those of a thermoregulating organism (and with live = 1 there will be metabolic heat generated and also heat lost by respiration and potentially the eyes, which isn't the case when live = 0).

All the best,
Mike

messages.author: 6cec8ea3702ece93
messages.subject: Re: Operative temperature
parts:
Hi Arielson,
It depends on whether you want the operative temperature of a behaving animal. If you want just the potential temperature of the animal sitting in e.g. the open, you can put 'live = 0' then you don't have to worry about changing those parameters you mentioned. Alternatively, you could put 'live = 1' and make the thresholds for activity etc. sufficiently large that they wont ever come into effect, and also make the organism diurnal,  nocturnal and crepusculsar, and that would give you a predicted body temperature that also includes effects of water loss rate and metabolic rate.
All the best,
Mike
